The distinction between invafidating an individual action 
improperly taken in rehance on a nonbinding policy statement and 
invafidating the poficy statement itself is important. As in the 
television commercial in which the automobile repairman intones 
ominously “pay me now, or pay me later,” the agency has a choice: It 
can go through the procedural effort of making a legislative rule now 
and avoid the burdens of case-by-case justification down the road, or 
it can avoid the hassle of rulemaking now, but at the price of having 
to engage in more extensive, case-by-case justification down the road. 
The central point is, however, that this is and should remain the 
agency's choice.
E. Donald Elliott, Re-Inventing Rulemaking, 41 DUKE. L.J. 1490, 1491 (1992). 
This proposal and others like it are dubbed “the short cut” and critiqued in 
David L. Franklin, Legislative Rules, Nonlegislative Rules, and the Perils of the 
Short Cut, 120 Ya l e L.J. 276 (2010). Among other criticisms, Franklin argues 
that the “short cut,” if followed by courts, would effectively prevent judicial 
review of deregulatory initiatives. If an agency issued guidance saying, “We 
if
shall no longer enforce provisions X, Y, or Z of our statute,” the subsequent 
'
enforcement action for which Elliott envisions judicial review would never 
•
occur. By contrast, such guidance could be reviewed if beneficiaries could sue 
the agency for promulgating what was effectively a legislative rule without 
notice and commentJ^ Hence, the “short cut” may disadvantage the 
beneficiaries of regulation (e.g., asthmatics breathing air pollution) as 
compared to regulated parties (e.g., power plants). In addition to the 
deregulation issue, one can argue more generally that (1) the short cut will 
render notice-and-comment proceedings less common—^proceedings that, being 
transparent and salient, give regulatory beneficiaries a higher level of access, 
relative to regulated parties, than do the more casual “insider” processes by 
which guidance is developed; and (2) the short cut will concentrate more review 
in ex-post enforcement actions—actions that by definition include regulated 
parties but are unlikely to include regulatory beneficiaries, due to procedural 
hurdles and resource constraints. See Nina A. Mendelson, Regulatory 
Beneficiaries and Informal Agency Policy making, 92 CORNELL L. Re v . 397, 
420-33 (2007).
2. Concerns About Guidance and Participation as a Remedy, It is 
commonly believed that, as notice-and-comment rulemaking became more 
burdensome due to the rise of “hard look” judicial review in the 1970s and 0MB 
rulemaking review in the 1980s, agencies’ resort to guidance increased as a 
means of making poficy without the burdens of notice and comment. This is
